meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Every time we liberate a woman, we liberate a man'?
meta.ogDescription: Attributed to Margaret Mead — the earliest trace is a 1967 newsletter quoting her. No primary Mead source has ever been produced.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Mead, and consistent with the argument she spent a career making — that the temperaments cultures assign to men and women are learned rather than given. But the earliest appearance anyone has located is a third party quoting her in a 1967 members’ newsletter, and no book, essay, column, letter or transcript of Mead’s own has been found containing the sentence.

source.excerpt: Every time we liberate a woman, we liberate a man.
trail: 1967 — the earliest appearance located. Wikiquote lists the line in the 1960s section of its Mead page with the citation “Attributed in La Abogada newsletter, Vol. 3 (1967) by International Federation of Women Lawyers, p. 5”. Note the phrasing Wikiquote itself chose: attributed in, not written in. Wikiquote: Margaret Mead ↗

La Abogada is a real publication — the newsletter of the International Federation of Women Lawyers, an organisation established in 1944 in Mexico City, issued four times a year in Spanish and English to members only. That makes the citation plausible, and also explains why it is so hard to check: a members-only newsletter is not a text most libraries hold. International Federation of Women Lawyers ↗

1982 — a biographer says she wrote it. Robert Cassidy’s Margaret Mead: A Voice for the Century carries the sentence followed by the words “she wrote” — but the surrounding text names no book, article or letter it was written in. A biographer’s bare assertion is a lead, not a source. The biography’s catalogue record: Universe Books, 1982 ↗

Everywhere else, it is anthology traffic. A full-text search of scanned books returns the sentence in quotation collections, business-advice books, a Virago feminism anthology and an interfaith Haggadah — every one crediting Mead, not one naming a source. Full-text search across scanned books ↗
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller passage to quote. Every located appearance is the sentence standing alone under Mead’s name, with no paragraph around it — which is itself the problem.

source.rightsNote: The line cannot be tied to any identified work, so no rights status can honestly be asserted. What can be said is what it is not: the earliest appearance located dates from 1967, far too late for any pre-1931 public-domain claim, so this should not be treated as public domain. If Mead did write or say it, rights would rest with her estate and with whatever publication first carried it.

author.name: Margaret Mead
author.heading: About Margaret Mead
author.metaLine: 1901–1978 · American cultural anthropologist, museum curator & public voice
author.bio: Margaret Mead was the anthropologist who made the discipline famous, beginning with Coming of Age in Samoa (1928) and continuing through Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935), which challenged the assumption that masculinity and femininity are fixed by nature. She served for years as a curator of ethnology at the American Museum of Natural History and, unusually for a scholar, wrote a monthly column in Redbook with Rhoda Métraux, becoming a genuine mass-media figure in the 1960s and 1970s. That reach is also why her attributions are so hard to pin down: she spoke in public constantly, and the record of what she said is scattered across magazines, lectures and newsletters rather than gathered in citable books.

misattribution.heading: Why this one needs an asterisk
misattribution.intro: No rival author has ever been proposed for this sentence, and no researcher has debunked it — Quote Investigator has no entry on it at all ↗. The trouble is narrower, and it is the standard trouble with Mead: she is one of the most quoted Americans of the twentieth century, and a great deal of what circulates under her name has never been traced to anything she published.

items.who: Margaret Mead — “Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed citizens can change the world”
items.why: Her single most famous line sits in Wikiquote’s Disputed section: attributed in Curing Nuclear Madness (1984) and later collections, with no contemporaneous source known, and with Ralph Keyes’ The Quote Verifier (2006) cited there as giving it as an example of derivative sources merely quoting each other. Wikiquote: Margaret Mead, Disputed ↗

On that “Never doubt” line, writers have noted it appears in none of her published books, letters, speeches or interviews — and that Mead’s own institute admits it has no idea where it came from. A famous name plus an appealing sentence is enough to keep a quotation alive with nothing underneath it. As Margaret Mead never said… ↗

Goodreads carries the sentence under Mead’s name with no source whatsoever, beneath a notice that its quotations are added by the community and are not verified — which is how most of the internet’s copies of this line were made. Goodreads: the quote, with no source ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The honest position: the sentence has been credited to Margaret Mead since at least 1967, nobody has offered a rival author, and nobody has produced a text of hers containing it. The only citation on record is La Abogada — a newsletter quoting her, not a work she wrote. Wikiquote records exactly that ↗

context.heading: Why the line travels
lead: The appeal is that it converts a zero-sum argument into a shared one: it tells men that women’s freedom is not something taken from them but something handed to them. That is why it turns up in such wildly unrelated places — quotation anthologies, business-advice books, a Virago feminism anthology, an interfaith Haggadah — wherever someone needs the shortest possible version of an idea that usually takes a paragraph. The scanned-book trail shows exactly that spread ↗

Mead is a plausible author for it. She spent a career challenging the assumption that masculinity and femininity are fixed by nature — the case she was already making in Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935) — which makes “liberating a man” a coherent thing for her to say rather than a slogan grafted onto her name. But plausibility is precisely how weak attributions survive, and it is not evidence. The strongest documentation anyone has produced is a 1967 newsletter quoting her, and a 1982 biographer saying she wrote it without saying where.
detailsBody: What would settle it is a copy of La Abogada, Vol. 3 (1967), p. 5. That page would show whether the newsletter cites a Mead article, a speech or a letter to the federation, or simply prints the sentence as an epigraph — the likeliest case, and one that would leave the trail exactly where it is now.
Until then the honest label is attributed: credited to Mead since at least 1967, contradicted by nobody, and confirmed by nothing.
context.pull: No rival author, no debunking — and no source either.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Margaret Mead page lists "Every time we liberate a woman, we liberate a man." in its 1960s section with the citation "Attributed in La Abogada newsletter, Vol. 3 (1967) by International Federation of Women Lawyers, p. 5".

Wikiquote's Disputed section places "Never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed citizens can change the world" there, noting it was attributed in Curing Nuclear Madness (1984), that no contemporaneous source is known, and that Ralph Keyes' The Quote Verifier (2006), p. xvi gives it as an example of derivative sources merely citing each other.
Quote Investigator has no article on "Every time we liberate a woman, we liberate a man" — a site search returns "Nothing Found".

Margaret Mead lived December 16, 1901 – November 15, 1978, was an American cultural anthropologist, author and speaker, served as curator of ethnology at the American Museum of Natural History, wrote a monthly Redbook column with Rhoda Métraux, and published Coming of Age in Samoa (1928) and Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935).

La Abogada is the newsletter of the International Federation of Women Lawyers, published four times a year in Spanish and English for members only; the federation was established in 1944 in Mexico City.
The "Never doubt that a small group..." quotation does not appear in any of Mead's published books, letters, speeches or interviews, and Mead's own institute admits it has no idea where it came from.

A full-text search of scanned books returns the sentence only in quotation anthologies, business-advice books, a Virago feminism anthology and an interfaith Haggadah, plus Robert Cassidy's Margaret Mead biography, whose snippet reads: "Every time we liberate a woman, we liberate a man," she wrote — with no source named.
Robert Cassidy's Margaret Mead: a voice for the century was first published in 1982 by Universe Books.
Goodreads carries the quote credited to Margaret Mead with no source work named, above a notice that its quotes are added by the community and are not verified.
LibQuotes gives the quote's source as "Attributed in La Abogada newsletter, Vol. 3 (1967) by International Federation of Women Lawyers, p. 5", matching the Wikiquote citation.
